source.summary: CVE-2026-114938 Java4Shell Write once, RCE everywhere Story by the New York Times A memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. A remote attacker with no credentials can overwrite heap memory, read it in the style of Heartbleed, and reach remote code execution. Begin ↓ Technical write-up ↘ Check your servers ↘ Recommendations ↘ After we disclosed PHP2Shell , we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java. Today, we are disclosing Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is the most popular Java runtime. Under CVSS 4.0, this vulnerability scores 9.2 out of 10 (CRITICAL). While PHP is a high-level web technology, Java sits much deeper. Java is the world's third most popular programming language , powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies . It is the beating heart of the modern economy. Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems. Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages. To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single = : Copy AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA= In older OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 128 of A followed by = . Write once, RCE everywhere Our initial testing demonstrated remote code execution in the following widely deployed Java applications, in their default configs. Pre-auth RCE: Keycloak Atlassian Jira Atlassian Confluence JFrog Artifactory Jenkins PingFederate Post-auth RCE: Apache Kafka Broker Apache Solr Elasticsearch Gerrit Spinnaker The lists are non-exhaustive. We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested. samczsun also shared a client-side exploit with us. A Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own. Here are a demo video of the exploits running: Wait, Java has a memory-corruption vulnerability, in Base64?! Yes. First time? Memory corruption is the most common class of vulnerability on the Internet. But one of Java's biggest selling points is memory safety. Java manages memory on developers' behalf and checks memory accesses, protecting applications from the memory-corruption bugs common in other software. But like PHP and many other technologies, much of Java itself is written in low-level languages like C, C++, and, in this case, assembly, where memory corruption is still a part of life. To speed up Base64 decoding, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors. The bug sits in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters. For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array. After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array. Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted. Era of the centaur hacker As with PHP2Shell, Calif used AI to find and weaponize Java4Shell. AI brings the horsepower. Our researchers bring the context. The best hacker today is neither AI nor human. It is the centaur hacker , part human, part AI. It took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit. The total token cost was less than $200. One thing to note about this vulnerability is that there is no universal exploit. Depending on how Base64 is used and how the application works, different steps may be required for exploitation. Calif was able to accelerate the exploit development by spending initial effort building pipelines and strategies, then directing AI agents to use those for initial exploitation. Afterwards, most of the later chains are built almost autonomously with AI. The tragedy of the commons Java is one of many shared software stacks we all rely on. Over the years, it has grown to serve many different needs. Each feature request may make sense on its own, but everyone inherits the added complexity. Those who need a feature get the benefit. Everyone else carries the code and its risks, even if they never use it. Java4Shell is a concrete example. The Base64 optimization helps applications that decode enormous amounts of data. But the code ships to everyone else too, including applications that gain little from it. On affected systems, an optimization few applications needed became a serious security risk. Features can be useful, and most bugs can be fixed. But why do we have to worry about code we never needed in the first place? A call for vibe-uncoding If you don't need something, there is little reason to keep it running in your systems. Do you need that hand-rolled assembly Base64 decoder to process a few hundred bytes? Probably not. Earlier this year we found Squidbleed , an older cousin of Heartbleed, hiding in the Squid proxy since 1997. The bug was in Squid's FTP module. But who uses FTP anymore? It's a dead protocol and should be removed. Removing code is harder than it sounds. An apparently unused feature may have hidden dependencies. Someone has to understand what can be removed, make the change, and test what remains. This is where AI can help to make that work practical at a scale we could not previously afford. The same centaur hacker that discovered PHP2Shell and Java4Shell can comb a large codebase and flag dead code, bloated features, and needless optimizations. We call this vibe-uncoding : identify the parts a system actually needs, then remove everything else to reduce its attack surface. With AI, everyone is asking, “What can we build?” But maybe the right question for security is, “What can we delete?” The Tail of Base64 By Quang Luong On affected OpenJDK builds, malformed Base64 data can cause a constant-value overwrite of allocated heap memory. Through remote Heap Feng Shui, we turn that overwrite into a heap leak and remote code execution. Discovery A few months back, I was developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. The bug was constrained: it is a linear out-of-bounds write and we have no way to bypass ASLR. I almost considered it unexploitable until I audited the Android Runtime. Turns out, it has some predictable memory allocation pattern and if you align the registers from the starting memory corruption just right you can make the runtime interpret attacker's bytecode. Lesson learned Complicated system interactions are hard, and this complexity can make exploiting hard bugs easy. After completing that exploit chain, inspired (and bored), I decided to look into some thing completely different. So I pulled the official JVM implementation (OpenJDK HotSpot) and started auditing. Java is a mature platform, so I was aware that having a "good" bug here would be hard, but I wanted to give it my best attempt anyway. Recalling my earlier lesson that complex systems and code crossing multiple boundaries are difficult to get right, I focused the audit on the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely accessible APIs, and cryptography. Well, more precisely, I told Codex to look at those areas like any serious security researcher in 2026. To be honest, I didn't expect to find anything trivially exploitable, perhaps only some logic flaws or side-channel issues. Most early results Codex brought me were slops, either unreachable or the requirement of exploitation is not realistic at all. This looks like a gamble I am going to lose. But you know what, fortune favors the bold. So I just prompted harder... Eventually, Codex brought me a finding for a memory corruption in the Base64 decoder itself. I came looking for copper and found gold, through sheer persistence. But wait, is it really gold, or just fool's gold? Note That sheer persistence is prompting AI and ignoring slops for around 20 minutes, by the way. The vulnerability The issue lies in OpenJDK HotSpot's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. C2 is the most aggressive JIT compiler in the Java Virtual Machine. Specifically, if you trigger a function repeatedly, then it will compile that function into native code. Even then, ordinary native code itself is not fast enough. Modern CPUs have specialized instructions that allow processing data even faster. HotSpot uses them in optimized routines called intrinsics. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic miscalculated the padded tail's store mask, causing an out-of-bounds write. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic iterates through the input in 256-byte blocks; if it is less than 256, then it will do so in 64-byte blocks. When the input is less than 64 bytes, it uses evmovdqub , the intrinsic for the VMOVDQU8 instruction. This instruction takes a 64-bit mask that decides which bytes are read from or written to memory. The mask is first calculated from the input and output length, then updated to reflect the number of padding bytes ( '=' ) in the Base64-encoded string. This is shown in the following (pseudocode): Copy // Zero High Bits Starting with Specified Bit Position input_mask := bzhiq(-1, input_length) output_len := (input_length / 4) * 3 // handle padding if input[input_length - 1] == '=': output_len -= 1 input_mask >>= 1 if input[input_length - 2] == '=': output_len -= 1 input_mask >>= 1 output_mask := bzhiq(-1, output_len) In the above code, if the remaining input is of the form =, ==, X=, X==, XY= , or === , then output_len will be computed as zero. However, since there is padding, output_len is decremented, resulting in an underflowed value of -1 or -2 . Since bzhiq(-1, output_len) doesn’t change any bits if output_len >= 64 , this results in output_mask == -1u64 . Later the code uses evmovdqub to read and write multiple bytes at a time. For a write, if the mask bit is 1 , the byte at that index in the vector register is written to memory. So when output_mask == -1u64 , all 64 bytes are written during the following operation: Copy evmovdqub( Address(dest, dp) /* Address: destination address addr */, k1 /* k1 == output_mask */, tmp /* XMMRegister src register/value to write */, true, Assembler::AVX_512bit /* vector length */ ); The generated stub returns the number of bytes it successfully decoded, and returns early when it detects invalid input. The remaining bytes are handled by the Java code, which throws IllegalArgumentException if the input is invalid. At runtime, the decoded buffer length is calculated as (ceil(inp_len / 4) * 3) - padding . When the bug is triggered, with 65 bytes ( [64 bytes] + '=' ) as input, that calculation allocates a 50 -byte buffer. During decoding the bug makes output_mask == -1 for evmovdqub , so 64 bytes are written starting at offset 48 , an out-of-bounds write past the end of the buffer. On OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 'A' * 128 + '=' instead of 'A' * 64 + '=' , because the length threshold to reach the code path is higher. Exploitation strategy The Base64 bug was gold, but not the type that sits on the riverbed waiting to be panned out. It was the type that was deep, dark, and hard to access. While we had memory corruption, exploiting it looked difficult, perhaps even borderline unexploitable, since it only wrote fixed bytes to the heap.
source.title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
